name: Sara Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sara, thanks for joining me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach design and technology at Fairfield School, a big secondary, and this is my second year. My classroom is a workshop: saws, a laser cutter, two 3D printers and a lot of sawdust. I love it when a Year 9 takes home a lamp they designed and wired themselves. I'm still learning the safety side, honestly, keeping twenty-two kids near band saws all in view at once, and my head of department pulled me up on it last month.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Josh, who works in his family's building firm, and we live in a house his parents helped us buy. I've got about ten months of savings and a small share in the firm. I'm a churchgoer, I believe in apprenticeships and people working for what they have. But I love tech: I use AI every day for designs, worksheets and to check my 3D models before printing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still really useful, just not the revolution people promised. I'd keep telling colleagues how much time it saves me on worksheets. I'd say kids still need to learn to make things with their hands, which was always true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. I keep using the tools, the workshop stays the workshop. The thing I actually need to sort out is my safety routines. One accident in my workshop would be the end of my teaching career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for planning and designs. I'd book myself on a workshop safety course in the spring term and ask my head of department to observe a practical lesson. We'd keep saving and maybe extend the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one accident would be the end of you. Has anything happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A near miss in October. A Year 8 boy reached across the bench drill while I was helping someone else, and the technician shouted. Nobody was hurt, but I didn't sleep that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to stay in teaching long term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, or maybe run training for apprentices at Josh's family firm later on. Teaching kids to make things is what I love. I'd like to set up a proper link between the school and local builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to value practical skills and apprenticeships again. I'd say kids should learn to use AI and a saw. I'd post about it on the school's D&T page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. D&T is mostly hands-on, and the design side is helped, not replaced, by AI. If anything, schools might put more money into practical subjects as desk jobs shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach students to design with AI and then build it by hand, starting this year. I'd ask the head to let me set up a link with Josh's firm for work experience. I'd keep investing in the family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. This is my subject's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said schools might put money into practical subjects. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd make the case to the governors myself. I'd show them the numbers: builders can't find apprentices, and kids want to do something real. If that fails, the firm always needs people who can teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, who works in insurance claims, which is all checking and answering customers. She'd be hit first. I'd tell her to look at trades, even if she laughs at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and businesses need to stick together and get people into practical work fast. I'd say government should fund apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd sound urgent but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the design part of my job goes by 2028, but the workshop doesn't, at least till robots come in 2031. After that I'm less sure: if robots can build, can they teach kids to build? I'd want to be somewhere that's training adults, not just kids, by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time assessor's qualification for construction apprenticeships right away. I'd help Josh's firm use AI for quotes and planning, because that's where they'd save money first. I'd keep my savings steady and put some into the firm's new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've got a plan and a family business behind me, but it's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots coming to building sites around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That worries me more than my own job, honestly. Josh's firm is all hands-on, and if robots lay bricks by 2032, his dad's business is in trouble. So we'd have three years to work out what the firm becomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn how things are made and how to fix them. A robot can lay bricks one day, but someone will still need to know when the wall is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is good time to build up apprenticeships and practical training. I'd say families and firms should plan together. I'd sound practical about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is plenty for me. I'd do the assessor qualification and start training apprentices part time for the firm. By 2031 I'd have one foot in school and one in the trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the assessor course next year. I'd keep teaching full time for now and help the firm bring in AI for quoting and scheduling. I'd talk with Josh's dad about the firm's plans for 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you talk to Josh's dad about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where the firm goes. Robots will find fixing and refitting old houses hardest, so that's where the family firm should go. And whether we start training our own apprentices. He's old-fashioned, but he listens to numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your own family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want children in the next few years. I'd probably go part time in teaching afterwards and do more with the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for practical people. Get kids into apprenticeships, get firms ready. I'd sound positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thrilled with ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, experienced in teaching, probably training apprentices too. Robots on sites come around 2039, and by then I'd have helped the firm get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep using AI every day. I'd build the school's link with local builders over the next few years. I'd do the assessor course at a gentle pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone you'd worry about with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The students. Kids who are told for ten years that everything's fine will be shocked when they find out it isn't. I'd want to be honest with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund apprenticeships and practical subjects, and let businesses train their own people. Fewer forms, more doing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, mostly for Josh's family firm, because the robots would come so soon after. What would help is proper funding for apprenticeships and help for small firms to retrain their own people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what children learn with their hands. If AI designs everything, a teenager still needs to feel a joint fit together. Making something real is how a kid learns that their effort matters.
